title: Jumping Flash!
subtitle: A rabbit above the landscape
summary: Jumping Flash! is Exact and Ultra's first-person platform game for PlayStation, released in Japan on 28 April 1995. Robbit, a mechanical rabbit, searches Crater Planet for jet pods stolen by Baron Aloha. Instead of watching a character cross the screen, the player looks through Robbit's eyes and launches high above the scenery. The combination makes height the main attraction: platforms become small landing places seen from the sky. Its bright islands and unusual viewpoint offered an early demonstration of how a console platformer could inhabit three dimensions.
body: Jumping Flash! is Exact and Ultra's first-person platform game for PlayStation, released in Japan on 28 April 1995. Robbit, a mechanical rabbit, searches Crater Planet for jet pods stolen by Baron Aloha. Instead of watching a character cross the screen, the player looks through Robbit's eyes and launches high above the scenery. The combination makes height the main attraction: platforms become small landing places seen from the sky. Its bright islands and unusual viewpoint offered an early demonstration of how a console platformer could inhabit three dimensions.

Robbit can jump three times before landing. The second and third leaps lift him far above the ground, while the camera tilts downward to show his shadow and the surface below. That movement solves a practical problem of first-person jumping: judging where the character will come down. A radar helps locate jet pods, enemies and items, and a timer keeps exploration moving. Looking around reveals the destination; the leap changes how that same space is understood, turning a distant ledge into a possible route through the stage.

A weak laser gives Robbit a regular attack, while collected fireworks provide stronger answers to enemies. Rockets, cherry bombs and other effects add bursts of colour to the journey. The game reused technology from Exact's earlier X68000 title Geograph Seal, adapting its first-person movement for PlayStation. Reviewers welcomed the graphics and unusual approach to platforming. Jumping Flash! 2 and Robbit Mon Dieu continued the character's adventures, but this first outing remains a particularly direct record of developers learning to make height, aiming and landing readable in a new kind of space.
